newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Arrest of South Korean bankers sought over Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: Arrest of South Korean bankers sought over Hanbo.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors on Wednesday appeared set to widen their probe into a scandal surrounding Hanbo Steel Co, saying they would seek to arrest the heads of some local banks over huge loans to the insolvent firm.

In a new twist to the unfolding scandal, a prominent opposition member of parliament said he had taken money from Chung Tae-soo, founder of the steelmaker's parent company Hanbo Group, partly to fund an election campaign.
Prosecutors last Friday arrested Chung on charges of fraud and violating laws on cheques and trust and savings companies.
"We plan to apply for arrest warrants against some bankers but I cannot say how many warrants will be sought," a prosecution official said.

He said Sheen Kwang-shik of Korea First Bank, Woo Chan-mok of Cho Hung Bank and Lee Hyung-koo, former chief of the state-run Korea Development Bank, were still being interrogated by state prosecutors after being summoned on Tuesday.
State radio earlier said prosecutors wanted to arrest Sheen and Woo on bribery charges.
The official declined to confirm the report. "I can only confirm that arrest warrants will be applied for today."

The three banks are main creditors of Hanbo Steel, which racked up about five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans from 61 banks and financial institutions before it was declared insolvent on January 23.

Prosecution officials said on Tuesday the bankers would be questioned on whether they received commissions in return for offering huge loans to Hanbo Steel, the country's second largest steelmaker and flagship of the Hanbo Group.

Politician Kwon Roh-kap, a close associate of opposition leader Kim Dae-jung, told reporters he had accepted between 150 million and 160 million won ($173,000-$184,000) from Hanbo founder Chung on three occasions since 1993.
Kim Dae-jung heads the main opposition National Congress for New Politics.
Asked by reporters about the nature of the money, Kwon said: "I believe they were either political funds or rice cake money. But I have nothing to do with preferential lendings to Hanbo."
South Koreans traditionally swap small amounts of money, known as rice cake money, or gifts during major holidays as a token of friendship or respect.
Kwon said part of the money was used to finance a party election in 1993.

He is the first politician to admit taking money from Chung, who built up South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate by rapidly expanding the steelmaker and by acquiring or setting up 18 companies in the past three years.
State prosecutors have questioned officials of Hanbo and its creditor banks over a lobbying fund kept by Chung and examined the conglomerate's bank accounts to check for irregularities.
They said the bankers under interrogation were asked if they had faced any pressure from politicians or government officials over the loans.
With presidential elections only 10 months away, the Hanbo loan scandal has emerged as a sensitive political issue.
President Kim, who ordered a probe into the loans last week, has called the scandal a typical example of corruption.
